headline_facts.claim: After adjusting for inflation, average published in-state tuition and fees at public four-year colleges rose from $3,230 in 1980-81 to $12,290 in 2026-27 (2026 dollars), about 3.8 times as much.
After adjusting for inflation, average published tuition and fees at private nonprofit four-year colleges rose from $14,610 in 1980-81 to $46,350 in 2026-27 (2026 dollars), about 3.2 times as much.
After adjusting for inflation, average published in-district tuition and fees at public two-year colleges rose from $1,570 in 1980-81 to $4,210 in 2026-27 (2026 dollars), about 2.7 times as much.
Real median household income rose from $61,690 in 1980 to $87,460 in 2025 (2025 dollars), an increase of about 42 percent.
The BLS consumer price index for college tuition and fees rose about 13.5-fold from 1980 to 2025 (annual averages), while the all-items CPI rose about 3.9-fold.

Indexed to 1980 = 100, by 2025 college tuition CPI stood at 1,349, nominal median household income at 494, nominal average hourly earnings of production and nonsupervisory workers at 458, and all-items CPI at 391.

Public four-year in-state tuition took about 117 hours of work at the average production and nonsupervisory wage in 1980-81 ($800 at $6.85 an hour) and about 381 hours in 2025-26 ($11,940 at $31.34 an hour).
Inflation-adjusted published tuition peaked around 2019-20 and has since fallen: public four-year in-state tuition was $13,580 in 2019-20 and 2020-21 versus $12,290 in 2026-27 (2026 dollars).
From 2015 to 2025 the college tuition CPI rose 21.6 percent, less than the 35.8 percent rise in the all-items CPI.

Average net tuition and fees after grant aid for first-time full-time in-state students at public four-year colleges fell from $4,170 in 2006-07 to an estimated $1,920 in 2026-27 (2026 dollars), as average grant aid nearly doubled to $10,370.
At private nonprofit four-year colleges, the estimated 2026-27 average net tuition and fees for first-time full-time students was $17,280, versus a published price of $46,350 (2026 dollars).

Average grant aid for first-time full-time public two-year students ($5,770 estimated in 2026-27) exceeds published tuition and fees ($4,210), so net tuition is negative, but the net cost of attendance including living costs is still about $16,230.
Students paid 20.9 percent of public colleges' total education revenue through net tuition in 1980 and 38.4 percent in 2025, after peaking at 47.5 percent in 2013.

Inflation-adjusted state and local education appropriations per public FTE student were $10,624 in 1980 and $12,082 in 2025 (2025 dollars, HECA-adjusted), while net tuition revenue per FTE rose from $2,808 to $7,459.

caveats: Sticker price is not what most students pay: College Board estimates that net tuition and fees after grants at public four-year colleges fell by more than half in real terms since 2006-07, and net prices for 2024-25 onward are projections, not observed data.

Net price figures cover first-time full-time students only and subtract grant aid, not loans, work-study or tax credits. The College Board long-run annual net price series only begins in 2006-07 in the 2026 edition; earlier years are not published there.
Real tuition at all three sectors has declined since about 2019-20, so a "still rising" framing is wrong for the last six years. The long-run claim (1980 onward) holds; the short-run one does not.

College Board constant dollars are deflated with CPI-U; Census real income uses R-CPI-U-RS and C-CPI-U; SHEEO uses HECA. Do not mix constant-dollar series on one axis without noting different deflators. The 1980=100 index series avoid this by staying nominal.
The tuition CPI (CUUR0000SEEB01) tracks published list prices for a fixed sample, not what students pay after aid, and it is not enrollment-weighted across sectors.
Median household income is for all households, not families with college-age children, and is a calendar-year measure while tuition is an academic-year measure (1980 means 1980-81 for tuition).

College Board and NCES differ in method: College Board weights by full-time undergraduate enrollment from its Annual Survey (1987-88 onward); NCES Table 330.10 weights by FTE undergraduates, does not adjust for residency, and uses 2023-24 dollars. Levels differ; trends agree.

College Board public two-year housing and food is not in its long-run table, so no long-run total cost series exists for that sector here; NCES gives only a combined 2-year figure for room and board where offered.

Rising published prices are partly offset by rising grant aid, and the student share of public college revenue grew partly because state funding per student fell after recessions (2001-2004, 2009-2012), then recovered. Appropriations are one driver among several (enrollment mix, out-of-state and graduate students, institutional spending).
NCES Digest 2024 Table 330.10 is the latest edition available; a Digest 2025 version of the table returned 404 on retrieval.

SHEEO SHEF annual data downloads are in nominal dollars; only selected years are published in constant (HECA) dollars in the report text and Table 2.1. The College Board CP-11B series (2024 dollars, 1994-95 onward) is the annual constant-dollar substitute.
unconfirmed: FRED series CUUR0000SEEB01 and CUSR0000SEEB01: FRED returned error pages for both on 2026-11-17, so the college tuition CPI was taken directly from BLS (same series id) instead. No FRED URL for it is cited.
Seasonally adjusted college tuition CPI (CUSR0000SEEB01): not retrieved; only the not seasonally adjusted annual averages are used, which is appropriate for annual comparisons.

An annual constant-dollar (HECA) SHEEO education appropriations per FTE series for every year 1980-2025: not available in the downloads opened; only nominal annual values and selected constant-dollar years were confirmed.
College Board net price annual series before 2006-07: not in the 2026 Excel workbook opened; not used.
BLS bulk download file (download.bls.gov cu.series) returned Access Denied; series values were obtained via the BLS public API instead.
